The agreement which created the Euro was written, sold to the people and signed with the clear idea behind it, that it establishes a joined currency that can not be manipulated by the individual states.

Obviously that means if a countries take up debt, it could not compensate it by printing more money, fucking over everybody in the process by devaluing the money.

This made people a little nervous, because they were worried that the problem of "giving away the candy, secretly stealing it back"-politics (this means you promise people money in the form of less taxes or more social security return for votes and then offset the hole in your budget by printing money so that it is not too obvious) would continue and mess states up.

So they came up with the idea of requiring all countries to meet certain benchmarks and be punished if they don't. They told their respective voters that the Euro was a good idea and that it would not mean they had to responsibility for the financial risks of other countries. There were serious doubts that this would work by some, in particular the school of "you have to spend money to make money, saving money means less growth", but it was put to work.

~~ A long while later ~~

Democracy worked it's magic and put forth some parliaments that were determined to make their budget work and others who did not. There was scolding for countries that missed the "stability criteria" and most of them did at some point. Some continued with their candy selling policy, others like Germany, found ways to move this off the books.

Remember the good Germans who did everything right? Yea, they found a fantastic way of dealing with this. You need to know that Germany has state organized retirement pay, but it is not capital based but on the "generation contract". This means that the people who work now pay the people who are retired now. So when it was invented you could hand out money for a couple generations who never paid in. Since it is not capital based but rather takes the money of the people now and promises them that other people will give them money in future, you can very easy fuck with it, cook the books a bit, make it look like it will be fine while actually handing out the candy and fucking over future generations. There are a couple other ways Germany took their candy off the books, but this one was a big one.

Other countries did not worry about these subtleties and just went on with the candy handing out straight. It showed up on their books and when the shit hit the fan, the people who borrow you money looked at Germany and said "looks fine to me" and then they looked at Greece and said "not so much". Interest rate were adjusted, the rest is history.

And then the American housing market imploded and ripped the world into a giant spiral of economic devastation

~~What now~~

The two schools are back on the table.

One group (aka the political left) wants to solve the problem by changing the original promise of the Euro and enable direct cash flow between the different partners while chipping away the right of the local governments to make financial decisions. This would probably work but you can not get the countries who end up paying (right now) more to agree on this because the popular vote will not carry it.

The other group says this will totally work out, we just have to keep a straight face while we break out own deal so our voters won't gut us and other states don't get bad ideas. If greece suffers, others will not think about following their path of "fuck it, we blow our money and let the others bail us out". Unfortunately the punishment also means that the economy is shot and we keep paying them because it does not work.

"Make people pay fines because they mismanaged their money means that they will have more money" is the dilemma and it comes down to the problem that every country will vote that they get the candy and the other ones the stones if you don't force them to act differently.

(PDF) A primer on questions and arguments re.Private contracting of govt services, including how to improve private contracting

I think it's very valuable, if one is arguing for increased private fulfillment of contracts, etc, to not just understand the various arguments that will often be presented by both sides.

But I think it is a missed opportunity to treat this subject, or use a paper like this, for only that - a set of rhetorical parrys and lunges.

Even more valuable is to seriously consider that this is a specialized form of the general extremely complex problem of improving efficiency and reliability (while contracting out and while not) within a large organization with many rules - something large businesses experience as well, though in a much different way.

I thought this was a relatively even-handed paper - when it presented both sides of an issue, it may have left some out, but it didn't, say, present one particular view as some "foil to argue against."

And I think reading it raised a lot of questions I hadn't even thought about before, but after thinking of them realized it was important to have an answer to. Example, this section below. Obviously there are too many requirements to be accountable to in modern government contracting, but I think even if pared them down a lot, for most public projects like infrastructure there has to be a standard of quality - at least when safety comes into play:

rivate contractors are hardly clamoring for oversight and regulation. They may tolerate some oversight, but they are saying that at some point oversight and accountability will be a deal breaker. They point out that there is always risk in contracting and say that terms to ensure that contracted-for services ar e provided at the cost agreed upon add to that risk, especially since it is difficult to write precise contracts when human services are involved. Indeed, some contractors and privatization proponents are rebelling against oversight. They reject the notion that they should be bound by contract to make the government or public whole when the contractor fails to live up to its obligations. This is a retreat from prior arguments in favor of privatization—that the contractor and not government would bear full responsibility for failure. As recently as 1998, an argument for privatization was framed thus:

Perhaps the most attractive feature of performance contracting is that risks don't fall so heavily on government but are shared more equitably between the agency and winning vendor. The vendor can be paid if and when the contracted-for objectives are achieved (e.g., more efficient revenue collections, lower unit service costs). Because of this, vendors are motivated to work closely with the agency to develop solutions that most quickly and feasibly deliver the outputs and outcomes sought. When both parties pursue the same goal and face risks together, they can work better together to create success.

Starting in about 2001, privatization proponents began to argue that contractors should be made less re sponsible for problems with their contractual performance. They contend that contractors are being asked to assume too much liability for perfo rmance problems and even to act as insurers of success. They say this bu rden will lead private companies to forgo opportunities, leading to less competition for projects.

Some privatization proponents express concern over having to provide guarantees or indemnification when problems arise with contracts. For example, Douglas Herbst, vice-president of CH2M HILL and chair of the National Council for Public-Private Partnerships, and David Mackenzie, an international transaction specialist, argue:

It’s clear that this trend toward over-the-top guarantees can’t continue as is. On future deals, contractors will negotiate ha rder, perhaps even walking away from terms they once accepted. Once this happens, the marketplace will have to adjust accordingly. The time when private companies push themselves away from the client’s tabl e because of unnecessary, excessive, and meaningless guarantee requirements may be near. And they need to be willing to do just that - if that’s what it takes to deliver the message.

Maximus, a large contractor, makes similar arguments. A guide to privatization’s pro’s and cons on Maximus’ website advises agencies not to make “the mistake of placing a contractor under the same restrictions, red tape, and bureaucratic constraint s of your government agency . . . .”

Of course, one person’s red tape is another’s accountability. When privatization proponents say that there should be no rules to determine what is permissible and no obligations to abide by contract terms, then constructing meaningful accountabilit y schemes will be an enormous battle. Private contractors will not voluntarily take on these obligations. If any accountability at all—certainly accountability at levels akin to that binding government—is to be imposed on contractors, the only route will be by legislation or through activist courts willing to overturn precedent on state action and standing.

Imposing accountability, by legislation or otherwise, is not cost- free. Contracting with government is voluntary, so a government that wants accountability may find itself with few bidders or agreeing to contract prices that will guarantee profits. For companies, as well as citizens, not all costs are monetary. Many contractors may not want to open their bank accounts to public review. When regulation means prices rise to a level at which a contractor cannot make a profit and perform the work for less than governme nt workers can, there is no point in privatizing. The only exception may be those companies for whom government work constitutes such a large part of their functions they would collapse if they no longer took it on
